title: Tie-dye, drag bingo, ice cream social | Here’s what’s happening in the Valley
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
With the fall semester beginning this week, it can be stressful dealing with a slew of fresh responsibilities. From moving in to course loads and new jobs, trying to find activities to take yourself away from the grind can fall to the bottom of your to-do list.

Fortunately, Penn State is offering several fun and engaging activities to help students ease into this new school year with a smile and a boost in spirits.

Here’s what’s happening in the valley this week.

Monday, August 24

Welcome To The Spiritual Center

University Park’s Center for Spiritual and Ethical Development is offering a welcome meetup for new and returning students to get to know one another, along with introducing the center’s staff and other affiliates.

Hosted at the Pasquerilla Spiritual Center, students can enjoy the iconic Penn State Berkey Creamery ice cream and create their very own novelty street sign. The activities aim to involve new students and help them get acclimated to Penn State. And, of course, its welcoming community.

This open house kicks off at 7 p.m. and runs until 9 p.m. No registration is required.

Drag Bingo

Part of Penn State’s “Welcome Week,” Drag Bingo is a staple of Happy Valley fun and is sure to deliver laughs and good vibes.

Featuring members of PSU Opulence, Penn State’s Drag Premier Ambassador Club, students will get to fuel their competitive fires with a rousing game of bingo and watch performances by members of Opulence.

Open from 7-9 p.m. with performers starting at 7:30, this event will be held at Alumni Hall in the HUB-Robeson Center.

Tuesday, August 25

Career Services Weekly Workshop

We’re all here to get our degrees, and we’re all looking to be employed post-graduation. Well, hopefully. Join Penn State’s Career Services Department for a workshop in building career skills for students’ futures both in and out of State College.

Hosted in the Bank of America Career Services Building, students will be led in professional development exercises including preparing for the career fair, receiving resume and cover letter tips and improvements, learning personal skill marketing for employers and preparing for internship and job searching and interviews.

If you can’t make it this week, fear not, as the workshop is available every Tuesday throughout the semester from 3:15 to 4 p.m.

Wednesday, August 26

Tie-Dye and De-Stress with CAPS

If you’ve unpacked your dorm and realized you don’t have enough clothes to fill your closet, you’re in luck. Penn State’s Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) wants to welcome students back to campus with a chance to get creative by making colorful, tie-dye tote bags.

There is no admission or bag charge, and students will get to de-stress and let the colors flow with their new merch.

This free event is being held on the HUB lawn from 12 to 2 p.m.

Feed the People Market Stand

Today, farm-fresh produce is a pricey and difficult commodity to find. So, why not stop by the info tables in the HUB for the Feed the People Market Stand?

This is a free market where students can enjoy fresh produce and learn more information on food access resources at Penn State.

The market is open every Wednesday from 2 to 4 p.m.

Pasquerilla & Dragons

In the mood for a little adventure? Then make the voyage over to the Pasquerilla Spiritual Center for a casual game of Dungeons and Dragons. Here, students can meet new warriors, wizards and druids for a night of fun and fantasy all while enjoying some free food.

This event is hosted every Wednesday night in the Pasquerilla Spiritual Center from 6 to 9 p.m.

Thursday, August 27

EcoReps Ice Cream Social

If you’re a first-year student, indulge your sweet tooth with a trip to either Pollock or Findlay Commons for an ice cream social.

Designed to help new students connect to Penn State Sustainability, this event is an informative and delicious way to get to know other students and staff at State College.

This social is another part of Penn State’s “Welcome Week” and will run from 6 to 8 p.m.

Campus Food System Kick-Off

For those looking to learn more about agriculture and sustainability, head over to the Campus Food System Kick-Off at the Student Farm on Big Hollow Road.

From 6 to 8 p.m., new and returning students will see the many opportunities to get involved in the new agriculture, nutrition, food systems and sustainability initiatives that Penn State has to offer.

Hosted by the Student Farm and Food Systems Department, this event is perfect for connecting students and staff with the resources they need to succeed in this field. Along with the showcase and networking, there will be free food.

Friday, August 28

“Pitch Perfect” at The State Theatre

Looking for an “aca-awesome” way to kick off your weekend? Then head down to The State Theatre for a viewing of the classic, 2012 box office hit “Pitch Perfect.”

The showing starts at 8 p.m. and students can purchase tickets at The State Theatre website or in person for $10.58. Who doesn’t love student discounts?

title: Position preview | Young returners, 1 veteran transfer highlight Penn State’s DE room
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
With Dani Dennis-Sutton moved on to the NFL, Penn State’s defensive end room is looking for its next star.

It’s a room that, unlike the majority of the team, doesn’t feature too many transfers, with just Ike Ezeogu from Iowa State and Alex McPherson from Colorado coming in from elsewhere. The room is also fairly young, and those younger players have battled throughout the offseason with some leading the pack for a starting spot.

Here’s a deeper look at what the defensive end room will look like, ahead of the 2026 season.

Potential starters

Out of all of the returning defensive ends, redshirt sophomore Max Granville has generated the most buzz as a potential starter, largely due to the story surrounding his return from injury.

Granville is back and practicing at fall camp, and the coaching staff have voiced their excitement for his potential breakout campaign. The nation has taken notice as well, naming him to the Comeback Player of the Year Award watch list.

Yvan Kemajou is in the mix for a starting role as well after a solid year in 2025 as a true freshman, where he recorded 13 tackles, five tackles for loss, 1.5 sacks and one pass breakup in 11 games.

Ezeogu, the only former Cyclone in the room, is also the oldest and most experienced player among them. The redshirt senior was a full-time starter for the first time in 2025 with career numbers of 60 tackles, six tackles for loss, three sacks, four pass breakups and a fumble recovery in 39 games.

Depth pieces

McPherson, the other transfer alongside Ezeogu, had an impressive true freshman season at Colorado last year. The 6-foot-6 defensive end played in 10 games, made 16 tackles, pressured the quarterback six times and blocked a punt against Delaware in Week 2.

LaVar Arrington II is also likely to see modest playing time after spending most of his true freshman year playing on special teams. This will be his first season at the defensive end position after switching from linebacker.

Redshirt junior Mason Robinson, redshirt sophomore Aidan Probst and redshirt freshman Dayshaun Burnett all haven’t seen action in their careers so far and will likely serve as depth pieces.

The lone true freshman

Penn State’s defensive end room has only one true freshman, Jackson Ford, who was the only player from the Nittany Lions’ original 2026 class to stay committed after James Franklin was fired.

The Malvern Prep product was a 4-star recruit and the No. 9 player out of Pennsylvania.

Ford got considerable praise from Matt Campbell on Thursday, who said Ford could be one of the new recruits that see serious playing time throughout the season — although he’ll likely see the field mostly on special teams.

“Ford has done a really good job through spring ball and then in the season, you're gonna have to fight to get yourself into a position at the defensive end,” Campbell said on Thursday. “I think Jackson can help us in some other ways too.”

title: Penn State wrestling's Jayden James earns U20 World Silver Medal
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Jayden James is returning to the United States with some hardware.

James earned the silver medal at the U20 World Championships at 74 kilograms in Bratislava, Slovakia.

The freshman began his quest for gold on Saturday, defeating Slovakia's Samuel Vokal, 11-0, in just 1:25.

James then had to face a former high school teammate of his, Italy's Alessio Perentin, and avenged a loss in folkstyle last year, defeating Perentin 7-5.

The Nittany Lion cruised into the finals in his next two matches, defeating Belarus' Artsiom Bolsun and Kazakhstan's Nurdaulet Seilbekov, 10-0 and 13-4, respectively.

James and Japan's Ariya Yoshida met in the finals and put together a high-scoring affair. James controlled a majority of the match, but gave up two takedowns with under 30 seconds remaining to lose the gold medal match, 13-12.

James will bring a silver medal back to State College just three months before he begins his collegiate career. The No. 3 recruit in the 2026 class, according to FloWrestling, is expected to wrestle at 165 or 174 pounds during his time at Penn State.

title: Position preview | Penn State’s DTs boast experienced veterans, new faces
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s defensive tackle room has many new faces taking the field this year.

While position battles are still underway, several athletes have stood out as potential starters, including Siale Taupaki, Keanu Williams, Armstrong Nnodim and Dallas Vakalahi.

Here's a look at Penn State's defensive tackles this season.

Veteran transfers

Matt Campbell earned a pair of commitments from experienced tackles in Taupaki and Williams, as the two combine for nearly 15 years of collegiate experience, with Taupaki entering his eighth season of eligibility.

Taupaki spent the last five seasons with the Bruins, including three seasons under Ikaika Malloe, who is now the defensive line coach for the Nittany Lions. He has only started eight games throughout his collegiate career, but made his biggest impacts in 2024 and 2025, where he combined for 38 tackles, three tackles for loss, two sacks and a fumble recovery.

On the other hand, Williams has spent the last five seasons bouncing around what is now the Big Ten. He began his career at Oregon, playing two years there before joining Taupaki at UCLA for three years.

Campbell has praised Williams throughout fall camp, saying on Aug. 13 that he’s “a guy that’s flashed every practice.”

Williams had his biggest year in 2025, where he recorded 39 tackles with the Bruins.

Young new pieces

Outside of the veteran transfers, Penn State also landed some new, younger players.

All three transfers are in their third year of college football, coming from Utah, Iowa State and Oklahoma State respectively.

Nnodim is the most likely starter of the trio, having spent the last two seasons with the Cowboys. He started in four games during his redshirt freshman year with an additional eight appearances, tallying 11 tackles, two tackles for loss and a sack.

While he was banged up heading into camp, Nnodim has gotten back into the swing of things and been one of the most energetic players on the team this year.

“He finally looks healthy here the last couple days,” Campbell said on Aug. 13. It’s going to be really fun to see what he continues to progress to.”

Vakalahi boasts very similar experience to Nnodim, having started five games during his two years at Utah. He didn’t see the field much during spring practice and sustained an injury toward the middle of fall camp that has kept him off the field, but Campbell said it was minor.

Former Iowa State defensive tackle Alijah Carnell is the last of the three transfers, having the least experience. Campbell had good things to say about Carnell during fall camp regarding his development over the two years.

“He’s a guy that’s been a real surprise for us,” Campbell said on Aug. 13. “He certainly made a huge play on the goal line yesterday which was really great to see.”

The one freshman of the new faces, Elijah Reeder, was committed to Campbell at Iowa State, but visited and pledged to Penn State after Campbell’s hiring. He was a 4-star and the No. 26 player at his position, per 247sports composite.

Returners

The Nittany Lions have four defensive tackles returning from last season, all of whom have little collegiate experience.

Ty Blanding is back for his fourth season at Penn State after seeing his most playing time last year. Blanding played in 13 games in 2025, making nine tackles and two tackles for loss.

Liam Andrews and De’Andre Cook both enter their third seasons in Happy Valley and have a combined nine appearances. Andrews, however, was working with the defensive ends at the end of the spring.

Caleb Brewer is also entering his redshirt sophomore year, but has not made an appearance for Penn State.

title: Penn State has garnered national attention after an alleged fraternity-led cocaine-trafficking ring bust. Here’s how it maps out.
author: Kahlie Wray & Mia Debelevich
description:
Editor’s Note: The Daily Collegian has an anonymous tip form for information on the fraternities, the individuals involved in the cocaine-trafficking ring, hazing and drug-use on campus. The Collegian encourages anyone with information to submit.

On Monday, 14 people, including 13 current and former Penn State students were arrested in a cocaine-trafficking ring bust tied to the Delta Upsilon and Sigma Chi fraternities.

Here’s what we know.

Who’s involved, and what are their charges?

Agostino Abbatiello

Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, is one of the two alleged leaders of the drug-ring. He’s a former Penn State student and member of the Sigma Chi fraternity, where he was an alleged main supplier.

“The consensus among the witnesses that testified before the Grand Jury is that Abbatiello was the main dealer of cocaine at Penn State during this timeframe and he was making considerable amounts of money in the business,” the criminal complaint read.

Abbatiello is facing 11 felony charges, including: dealing in proceeds of unlawful activities with intent to promote the carrying on of the unlawful activity; criminal use of communication facility; conspiracy - manufacture, delivery, or possession; and seven counts of manufacture, delivery, or possession with intent to manufacture or deliver.

Allegedly, he regularly traveled to New York to acquire cocaine, which he cut and packaged primarily at Sigma Chi fraternity’s off-campus house. It was sold primarily to other Penn State students. Abbatiello also allegedly made pledges — new members of the fraternity — cut and package the cocaine as a hazing ritual.

According to the grand jury presentment, Abbatiello continued to distribute cocaine as recently as February 2026.

His alleged brother Sebastiano M. Abbatiello was charged on Thursday after allegedly being found with cocaine on a boat. It is not yet known if Sebastiano was involved in the alleged drug-trafficking ring tied to the fraternities.

Thomas Robinson

Thomas Robinson, 23, of Pittsburgh, is the other alleged leader of the ring. He’s a former Penn State student and member of the Delta Upsilon fraternity. According to the grand jury presentment, he sold cocaine from the fraternity’s off-campus house.

Upon his arrest, Robinson told police that Agostino was his source for cocaine. Robinson's first two purchases from Agostino were between six to eight ounces each; the third was 500 grams for $18,000; and he purchased one kilogram for $22,000 on two separate occasions, according to the grand jury presentment. These transactions took place from January to September 2024.

He is charged with 21 felonies, including: dealing in proceeds of unlawful activities with intent to promote the carrying on of the unlawful activity; five counts of criminal use of communication facility; and 13 counts of manufacture, delivery, or possession with intent to manufacture or deliver.

He is also charged with seven counts of intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered, a misdemeanor charge.

Mohammed Huraibi

Huraibi, 22, of Secaucus, New Jersey, is one of the Delta Upsilon brothers accused of purchasing cocaine from Agostino and repackaging at the fraternity house for profit.

According to the grand jury presentment, Huraibi introduced Robinson to cocaine at the house, and later asked if Robinson would become his business partner in distributing cocaine. Huraibi told Robinson that he wanted to back out of the operation in December 2023.

Though the current Penn State student allegedly distanced himself from the business, he continued selling to a friend.

He’s charged with four felonies: conspiracy - manufacture, delivery, or possession; dealing in proceeds of unlawful activities with intent to promote the carrying on of the unlawful activity; and criminal use of communication facility.

Huraibi is also charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Lars Zeepvat

Lars Zeepvat, 24, of Mendham, New Jersey, is a former Penn State student. He alleges Agostino loaned him $1500 for a spring break trip and made Zeepvat deliver cocaine for him to settle the debt, according to the grand jury presentment. On one occasion, Zeepvat allegedly traveled to New York to purchase cocaine for Abatiello.

The Sigma Chi brother is charged with four felonies, including: corrupt organizations - employee; conspiracy - manufacture, delivery, or possession with intent to manufacture or deliver; dealing in proceeds of unlawful activities with intent to promote the carrying on of the unlawful activity; and criminal use of communication facility.

He’s also charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Zeepvat is awaiting formal arraignment after waiving his preliminary hearing. He intends to plead not guilty, according to a signed waiver. His formal arraignment is scheduled for Sept. 9 and will take place at the Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte, Pennsylvania.

Robert Zanolla

Zanolla, 24, of Manhasset, New York, is a former student. Zanolla allegedly travelled with Zeepvat to purchase cocaine for Agostino in New York.

He’s charged with two felonies: conspiracy - manufacture, delivery, or possession with the intent to manufacture or deliver; and criminal use of communication facility.

Zanolla is also charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Kaden Howe

Howe, 22, of Monmouth Junction, New Jersey, was a known supplier of cocaine to his Acacia fraternity brothers, according to the grand jury presentment.

The current student is charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Liam Smith

Smith, 23, of Garden City, New York, is a former Penn State student. He allegedly assisted Agostino, his former roommate, in preparing the cocaine for distribution.

He’s charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Michael Brogno

Brogno, 20, of Ellicott City, Maryland, is a current student. Brogno, a Delta Upsilon brother, allegedly assisted Robinson by packaging and delivering the cocaine to customers.

He is charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Connor Hurleigh

Hurleigh, 22, of Oakdale, New York, also allegedly packaged and delivered cocaine to customers.

The current student and Delta Upsilon brother is charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Seth Beardsley

Beardsley, 20, of Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania, is a current student.

He’s charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Kyle Ridpath

Kyle Ridpath, 21, of Springfield, Pennsylvania, is a former Penn State student.

He’s charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Daniel Price

Daniel Price, 21, of Philadelphia, is a current student.

He’s charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Charlie Weisman

Weisman, of Mount Airy, Maryland, is a current student. His age is not listed in available court documents.

He’s charged with two misdemeanors: intentional possession of a controlled substance by person not registered; and use/possession of drug paraphernalia.

Paul Robinson

Paul Robinson, 59, of Pittsburgh, is the father of Thomas Robinson. He’s a managing attorney at Meyer, Darragh, Buckler, Bebeneck & Eck PLLC. According to reporting from TribLive, he was still practicing law as of Thursday.

He’s charged with one felony charge of hindering apprehension or prosecution - concealing or destroying evidence. Robinson is also charged with two misdemeanors, including: tampering with or fabricating physical evidence; and obstructing the administration of law or other governmental function.

How the investigation unraveled

The investigation began in September 2024, according to the criminal complaint. Det. Donald Paul developed confidential informants (CI) to purchase cocaine from Thomas Robinson at the Delta Upsilon fraternity house from September 2024 to December 2024.

After several purchases by the CI, totaling 73.8 grams of cocaine, Thomas was arrested, the complaint said. Thomas also allegedly used his full name on Venmo to accept payment for the drug.He allegedly cooperated with law enforcement following his arrest and told them Agostino was his source for cocaine.

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday announced the charges of the fourteen individuals involved during a press conference on Monday.

“This was a coordinated and highly-profitable drug-trafficking crew revolving around two senior members of the fraternities, other fraternity brothers, and pledges,” Sunday said in a Monday press release. “In fact, according to the evidence uncovered, cutting and packaging cocaine was, for some pledges, an indoctrination into the fraternities.”

Agostino, the alleged ring-leader, turned himself in on Tuesday and was denied bail at his arraignment. The prosecution will be led by the Office of Attorney General Drug Strike Force Section.

How the university responded

The university first responded to the allegations in a public news release on Monday.

“We are horrified by these serious allegations against current and former students,” Andrea Dowhower, vice president for Student Affairs, said in the release. “Criminal activity, including hazing, such as this has no place at our institution, and we will cooperate with law enforcement in any way we can. We will continue to enhance our efforts around health and safety and hazing educational efforts for all our organizations.”

The release stated Penn State would initiate its own investigation into the organizations and individuals involved. Current students and Delta Upsilon will undergo review in accordance with the university's conduct process, according to the release, and the fraternity has been placed on interim suspension. However, Sigma Chi operates outside of the university’s oversight as of 2021, when it was suspended, and will not be included in Penn State’s investigation process.

Penn State issued a second release on Friday announcing plans to introduce enhanced efforts to educate students about hazing, alcohol and drug-use prevention.

“These enhanced efforts, which will be shared in the next several weeks, include a parent education video, a hazing prevention education campaign, our annual messaging to student leaders and outreach efforts for harm reduction related to drug use,” Dowhower said in the release.

What does Penn State mean when it says Sigma Chi operates outside of university oversight?

In March 2025, three independent fraternities — Pi Kappa Alpha, Tau Kappa Epsilon and Sigma Chi — announced the creation of the State College Interfraternity Council (SCIFC). Sigma Pi and Acacia were added in September 2025.

The student-run council oversees Greek life of several non-university affiliated fraternities in State College, Pennsylvania. As the fraternities do not have official recognition from the university, Penn State does not oversee their operations.

The council was partially created so the fraternities would not have to adhere to reforms Penn State implemented after a 2019 agreement with the Piazza family, following the death of Timothy Piazza at the Beta Theta Pi fraternity house in 2017.

All fraternities in the council have hazing and misconduct allegations, according to Penn State’s hazing transparency report, which spans from 2021 to 2026.

“The university received a report including multiple photographs and videos of alleged hazing behaviors that occurred at Sigma Chi during the 2023-2024 academic year. The images and videos depicted individuals with tape and plastic covering their faces and being painted on with roller, individuals face-down with their hands behind their back with their face in food or vomit, and an individual in a wire dog kennel having unknown substances poured over him,” the hazing transparency report read.

A September 2025 SCIFC press release said all members of SCIFC organizations were required to complete a “mandatory, pre-semester training (to establish) a unified and proactive approach to event safety and responsible chapter management” with Standing Stone Consulting, an event security and risk management service.

Public response

Since Sunday announced the allegations on Monday, there’s been mixed reactions. Abbatiello has been dubbed “Pablo Pledgescobar” by social media users, and his image has been the subject of multiple memes.

In contrast, residents and State College Borough Council members are calling for Greek Life reform and public address.

In a public comment during the council’s Monday meeting, Highlands Civic Association President Mark Huncik said he would like to see Penn State address the borough regarding off-campus fraternities. Huncik said he’s in favor of a public forum where off-campus fraternities operating within the borough, regardless of whether they are recognized by Penn State or operating independently, can address concerts from local residents.

“We really need to understand the significant breadth of this security issue on the safety of our neighborhood,” Huncik said. “I think we need to take more of a proactive approach for something like this … so that there's a sharing of information as far as what the borough understands is going on, what Penn State understands is going on and what will happen as we move towards, hopefully, a much more safer and much more respectful future within the activities that are associated with our fraternity system within our neighborhood.”

Susan Venegoni, a council member, shared similar sentiments.

“Off campus is not off the radar,” Venegoni said. “It's in our community and I want someone to come and explain to us what we're doing with the fraternities in this community.”

What happens next?

For the 14 charged, preliminary hearings, court proceedings where a judge determines whether there is enough evidence for a case to proceed, are next.

Abbatiello, Huraibi, Zanolla and the Robinsons have preliminary hearings scheduled for Sept. 2. Weisman, Smith, Ridpath, Price, Hurleigh, Howe, Brogno and Beardsley have preliminary hearings scheduled for Oct. 14.

The preliminary hearings will have one of two results: The charges get dismissed, or the case proceeds. If the judge decides there is no probable cause, the court will dismiss the charges. If the judge decides there is probable cause, the case will move forward and a trial date will be set.

Jonathon Chiu, Geraldine Cruz-Hernandez and Victoria Pugh contributed reporting.

title: Penn State Health doctor dead after plane collides with Pa. State Police helicopter
author: Saxtyn Lutz | News Editor
description:
Paul Sokoloski, 57, of Hershey, Pennsylvania, died after a two-seat Cessna 150 he was piloting collided with a Pennsylvania State Police helicopter on Wednesday at Carlisle Regional Airport, according to a statement from state police.

Sokoloski was an emergency medicine physician for Penn State Health.

As the plane was landing on the runway, the Cessna unexpectedly veered off to the right, hitting the backside of the police helicopter, according to the statement. The helicopter was completing a training exercise above the grass next to the runway.

The statement said two troopers aboard the helicopter were injured.

“The Troop H Major Case Team was activated to assist with the investigation being conducted by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), in collaboration with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA),” the statement read.

Sokoloski worked for Penn State Health for 11 years, per his LinkedIn profile.

“The Penn State Health community is deeply saddened by the loss of Dr. Paul Sokoloski, a valued member of our emergency medicine team,” a statement from Penn State Health read. "Our thoughts are with his family, friends and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time. We are focused on supporting Dr. Sokoloski’s loved ones and the members of our care teams who worked alongside him and are grieving his passing."

title: Alleged drug-ring leader’s brother charged after being found on boat with cocaine in Centre County
author: Mia Debelevich | Managing Editor
description:
Editor’s Note: This story was updated Friday evening to include information on Abbatiello's enrollment status.

Sebastiano M. Abbatiello has been charged with three misdemeanors after allegedly being found with cocaine on a boat in Centre County on Thursday, according to court documents.

Sebastiano is the brother of Agostino Abbatiello, one of two alleged fraternity cocaine-trafficking ring leaders charged on Monday. Agostino is facing 11 felony charges.

Sebastiano was arrested by the Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission. He was charged with being unable to safely operate watercraft due to alcohol or drugs; drug use or possession; and intentional possession of a controlled substance by a person not registered.

He is currently enrolled as a Penn State student, Wyatt Dubois, a Penn State spokesperson, told The Daily Collegian. Dubois said the Office of Student Accountability and Conflict Response is currently reviewing the allegations, and the university may take student conduct action separate from the legal charges.

title: Penn State to enhance Greek life education following drug bust
author: Mia Debelevich | Managing Editor
description:
Penn State Student Affairs issued a statement saying the university plans to enhance efforts around fraternity and sorority education for students, according to a statement released Friday afternoon.

The statement follows a cocaine-trafficking ring bust tied to the Delta Upsilon and Sigma Chi fraternities, in which 14 people, including 13 former and current students, were arrested.

title: Alpha Phi Delta fraternity sues Greek housing organizations
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Alpha Phi Delta Fraternity filed a lawsuit on Thursday against 329 Prospect Avenue Corp. and Greek Housing Services Corporation after members of the fraternity were locked out of its off-campus fraternity house for move-in day earlier this week.

Mark Maloney, president of Greek Housing Services, told the fraternity that members would not be able to access the house because the organization was in default, Carolyn Fenton, the fraternity’s attorney, wrote in the lawsuit.

Allegedly, one member who scheduled to move into the house on Tuesday is a Type-1 diabetic whose insulin required refrigeration. The suit alleges that Maloney instructed workers to place a refrigerator outside, on the porch, instead of allowing access to the house.

In a March letter to Alpha Phi Delta members, President Andrew Steinkamp described the fraternity’s 2026-27 housing situation as a “developing crisis.” At the time, members of the fraternity had signed 27 total housing agreements, with its master lease agreement citing the minimum required at 55.

Fenton wrote that the fraternity “did not secure the requisite number of leases,” but the master lease agreement does not have a provision to address that scenario.

The lawsuit also said the fraternity is seeking an additional $5,000 from Greek Housing Services in the lawsuit after a renovation of the house’s third-floor bathroom was allegedly not completed by the established Aug. 18 deadline.

Alpha Phi Delta is seeking an emergency preliminary injunction to gain access to the house. A hearing is set for Tuesday at 3:30 p.m.

title: 3 Penn State players named to Comeback Player of the Year Award watch list

description:

title: Penn State RBs recognizing pass protection, ball security as ‘two most important things’ at position
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s running back room may have an all-around aspect to it that hasn’t been seen in prior years.

The biggest reason for that is the rushers ability to block, proving to be one of the most important ways to get on the field in running back coach Savon Huggins’ eyes.

“The two most important things as a running back is to protect the ball and protect the quarterback,” Huggins said. “That is a non-negotiable. If you can't do that, then you're gonna put yourself in a position to not play.”

The emphasis to protect the quarterback is not something that’ll show up on the scoresheet after the game, but can be a key to success for the overall offense, and potential NFL careers.

The individual running backs — who’ve taken a togetherness approach to the room rather than each individual — have also shown selflessness by putting their body on the line to protect the quarterback.

That ideology has already been put to work, with Carson Hansen recognizing that “ball security and protecting the quarterback are the two most important things,” which matches exactly what Huggins said.

Hansen’s a running back who’s had top-back numbers, nearly eclipsing 1,000 yards on the ground a season ago. However, those numbers don’t mean anything if he’s not also fending off additional blitzers to help keep the pocket clean in the pass game.

The focus on pass protection from the running backs is even more important when Rocco Becht is the one behind the line, who’s coming off shoulder surgery in the offseason.

Without Becht behind center, the Nittany Lions would lose not only a veteran quarterback, but one of their top leaders, something that’s been heavily talked about among his peers in the spring and summer.

Just a season ago, Kaytron Allen and Nick Singleton were praised for his pass protection, and Allen has stood out in his first NFL training camp as a blocker. It’s what James Peoples is striving for to make himself truly a complete running back with the running game, receiving game and pass protection culminating in a true top running back.

“It just more completes me as a running back,” Peoples said. “That's been something that I've really been working on, that I've really been stressing, and to see it paying off now by the reps, the countless reps that I was in here or not in here, and the film study is it's been great to see. So I’m continuing to get better at that, continue to emphasize that in my game, so that's a strength for me, one of the strongest pieces of my game.”

Whether it’s Peoples, Hansen or even Quinton Martin Jr. and Cam Wallace, who both are returning members of the room, the unit has continued to focus on pass protection.

The work they’ve put in at practice on pass protection has Huggins confident in all four of them to pick up rushers at any point during the regular season.

“I think all four of those guys have done an unbelievable job of sticking their face in there and being consistent with that,” Huggins said.

title: Penn State men's soccer overcomes 2 goal deficit in season opener, earning first win under coach Rob Dow
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions hosted the Mercyhurst Lakers for the opening match at Jeffrey Field on Thursday and the first under coach Rob Dow’s leadership with the blue and white. Penn State previously won 5-0 in last season's regular-season matchup against the Lakers in what is historically a favorable matchup; despite all the changes, the success continued.

Happy Valley was showered with heavy rain throughout the day, but the skies cleared out by kick-off, and what resulted was a thriller on the pitch, with Penn State pulling out a 3-2 win.

The goalkeeper began the game with a long clearance downfield, followed by an offensive push leading to a corner kick, and the Mercyhurst keeper collected the first set piece of the day for the white and blue.

Within the first five minutes of the game, both the back line and midfield were able to find passes to the attackers patiently. Mercyhurst played a low defensive line, allowing passes behind the half-field to go without pressure.

Penn State, however, approached their defense with more urgency, as attackers pressured the ball and forced Mercyhurst defenders to make decisions quickly.

Yet, the Lakers did just that. A long ball to their right-winger jump-started their first chance of the game. A run in the box led to the first shot on goal in the match, saved by Penn State goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese.

Mercyhurst then challenged the no-call, believing that the attacker was fouled in the box. The challenge was successful, and the Lakers cashed it in with a goal from the penalty spot to take a 1-0 lead with 37 minutes to go in the first half.

One challenge followed another, as Dow challenged a potential foul in the box. He received a different outcome, as the challenge was unsuccessful.

While Mercyhurst continued to hold its lead, Penn State continued to play with intensity on both ends of the field as its high press led to intercepted passes. Once gaining possession, the Nittany Lions earned their first shot of the game on a cross from the left side of their attack.

This trend continued throughout the half. After Mercyhurst’s first goal, the possession was dominated by the Nittany Lions. Mercyhurst’s attackers kept dropping deep, allowing for the Penn State defenders to find passes. The attack would also begin to string passes together in the final third.

Defender Toby Grant received a corner kick near the top of the box, then headed the ball back in the mix, leading to a shot on goal for midfielder Luca Sowinski.

Another key mistake for the Nittany Lions would come at the 26th minute of the match when a misplaced pass sent backward at the defense didn’t reach its target and allowed Mercyhurst to pounce on the opportunity, scoring its second goal of the half.

Even with a two-goal deficit, the white and blue did not let its heads down. Multiple chances were created through set pieces and crosses from the wing, but they simply couldn’t be finished.

The Nittany Lions finally punched in their first goal of the season, as defender Noah Förster sent a beautiful through ball to forward Amadou Kone, who took two touches and scored with 9 minutes left in the half.

Mercyhurst held possession for most of the remaining minutes before halftime, as Penn State headed into the break down 2-0. The scoreboard didn’t reflect the Nittany Lions first-half urgency, as they held a seven-to-three advantage in shots on goal.

After the second half kick-off, it was clear that Penn State didn’t want to take its foot off the gas pedal. Nehan Hasan immediately made a run through defenders, leading to two shots on goal in the first few seconds of the second half.

Goal-scoring opportunities continued to emerge for the Nittany Lions. Several corner kicks reached the heads of attackers, but none could reach the back of the net.

The first major foul of the game was given to Mercyhurst when the attacker recklessly contested a header from a goal kick, leading to a yellow card. The referee reviewed the play and upgraded the foul to a red card, forcing the Lakers to play with 10 men.

Penn State controlled the pace throughout the first 15 minutes of the second half. The Nittany Lions ability to win back the ball after shots on goal, along with Mercyhurst’s decision to allow blue and white defenders to possess the ball freely, led to various corner kicks and shot attempts.

Defender Joe Buckley fell to the ground, appearing to hold his right ankle with 24 minutes left in the game. The sophomore was able to get up and walk gingerly up the field, but was later substituted and taken off the field.

Penn State would finally convert their 17th shot attempt of the game, as defender Joe Sheridan finished a corner kick sent in by midfielder Grant McIntosh in the 68th minute, tying the game at 2-2.

Within five minutes, multiple players on both teams fell to the ground due to cramps, resulting in the referee stopping play on numerous occasions. However, Sheridan would be the only player in that time frame to come off the field. After a brief stretch on the sideline and assistance from trainers, he would immediately return to the action.

Mercyhurst defended on its half of the pitch for most of the second half, but once they won the ball near midfield, they pushed ahead for a fast break opportunity. Mercyhurst strung together a few passes before Peluffo-Wiese saved the Lakers’ shot attempt.

Mercyhurst continued to add to their poor second-half performance by conceding an own goal with six minutes remaining to give the Nittany Lions a 3-2 lead.

During the final five minutes of the match, Mercyhurst applied offensive pressure, creating multiple chances and taking shots. Despite that, the Penn State defense refused to allow the Lakers to tie the game.

title: No. 23 Penn State women's soccer continues season opening road trip with defeat to No. 22 West Virginia
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
After opening the season with a narrow draw against No. 2 Notre Dame, the blue and white trekked to Morgantown to continue the season on the road against a formidable West Virginia squad.

With coach Erica Dambach still sitting at 299 career wins, Penn State again entered on milestone watch, but couldn’t seize the moment for their manager, losing with a 2-1 result.

The Mountaineers began play with a deep ball into Penn State’s half, and that would signal much more of what would come in the opening 10 minutes. The blue and white got its first chance through goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress, who was under pressure with the ball outside the box and played it upfield for an attack that led to a cross the West Virginia keeper had to grab.

The Mountaineers soon thereafter got a chance inside the Penn State box, but with defenders swarming, the shot attempt soared over the bar. The Nittany Lions became the first to strike after both teams’ inaugural challenges when again it deployed a counterattack that quickly got into West Virginia’s final third.

Forward Paige Kalal picked up possession, drove toward the edge of the box and found attacking partner, freshman Anna Babcock, who powered a low driven shot for the first score of the season in her first career start.

Play went back and forth with both squads trading chances, but nothing was clear-cut, as the best attempt was a point-blank shot at Gress that went right into her hands. With a little over 13 minutes left to play in the first half, both teams opted for four changes, as coach Dambach brought on Kennedy Ring, Lilly Burger, Paige Pasinski and Kaelyn Wolfe.

A little over a minute later, the Mountaineers pulled even on a worldie scored by Olivia Shertzer, who smashed a shot from deep outside the box that went bar down with little to no chance of Gress stopping it.

That would mark most of the action before the break in what was a physical first half. Penn State committed five fouls to West Virginia’s seven, with the teams even with five shots.

After not even a minute into the second half, the Mountaineers got another chance but again skied the shot over the bar, as the tempo after the break favored the hosts. After appearing on the bench to start the second, Burger reentered to replace Lily Boyden.

Soon thereafter, Penn State found its way down to West Virginia’s half and earned the first corner kick of the game, but the attempt by Kalal went right at the side netting. The Nittany Lions’ tide continued to turn with a through ball that played to the Mountaineers goalkeeper, as they maintained a threat.

That threat fizzled out as the game stagnated, with no team able to generate chances until a stoppage with 27 minutes remaining to allow Pasinski and Wolfe to reenter.

After a few minutes elapsed, West Virginia finally broke through the Penn State defense. With the ball wide, the Mountaineers whipped a low-bouncing cross that bounced back post to an unmarked defender for an open-net tap-in that left multiple defenders with their heads in their hands.

The Nittany Lions attempted a challenge to no avail, and less than two minutes later the refs went back to the video board for a potential West Virginia foul in the box, but the review didn’t go Penn State’s way.

As the clock ticked down, chances also narrowed, as fatigue clearly began to set in with the deadlocked tie still not broken or even beginning to tip either way.

Penn State kept its foot on the pedal, but despite advantageous cornerkick situations, late substitutions and a last-minute shot at the edge of the box that just soared wide, it didn’t translate to goals, as the Nittany Lions finished still in search of their first victory.

title: ‘He’s not scared of anything’ | Penn State QB Alex Manske returns after open heart surgery
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Alex Manske didn’t have the same start at Penn State as the rest of Matt Campbell’s transfer class.

During medical testing performed on new athletes in the winter, Manske was diagnosed with a potentially fatal heart condition — a dilated aortic root and dilated ascending aorta he discovered from a routine echocardiogram in February.

Immediately following the diagnosis, Manske met with Campbell and the team’s medical staff to determine how he could return to football. On March 16, he underwent open heart surgery at the Mayo Clinic, where the doctors replaced his bicuspid aortic valve with an artificial graft.

“To watch him emotionally, mentally, the taxing aspect of are you even going to be able to play football again,” Campbell said Thursday. “He’s worked so hard to get to this point, knowing what that family went through.”

Less than two months after his surgery, Manske returned to Happy Valley in late April and was cleared for football activities two months later. Over the last two weeks of fall camp, he’s been a full participant and is slated to be the backup quarterback come Week 1.

From the moment Manske was diagnosed in February to his recovery during the spring and summer months, Campbell said there were “some scary moments.”

At the time, it was unknown whether Manske would return to play football. Now, he’s in the same position as the rest of Penn State’s quarterbacks and is practicing as if the condition was a thing of the past.

“I’d say it’s just what it was before,” Manske said Thursday. “The doctors are saying, the trainers are saying I’m good. They’re really just treating me like I was before.”

Since Manske was away in the spring, he didn’t experience Blue-White Practice, so last Saturday’s team scrimmage was his first time playing in Beaver Stadium.

Manske didn’t take the scrimmage lightly, asking quarterbacks coach Jake Waters the night before to “hit me, specifically in the chest,” during the practice.

“I’m giving him hits and all that because he wants to feel that,” Waters said Thursday. “He’s not scared of anything. There’s no limitations on him, but his mindset is ‘please hit me in the chest, I need to feel it.’”

As Manske was also recovering from injury when he arrived at Iowa State in 2025, the coaching staff has yet to have a full offseason and preseason with him practicing. During the last few weeks of practice, however, he’s proved his capability and his position as a future quarterback for the Nittany Lions.

“It tells you the mentality of this kid, not only to be able to go through it, but where he is today,” Campbell said. "It’s a miracle, it’s a blessing. We’re all really grateful for it.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell talks team identity, depth
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
On a rainy morning in State College, Matt Campbell took to the podium to speak with local media.

Campbell evaluated where the team’s identity is at this point in fall camp, touched on his excitement for the versatility in the roster and discussed notable freshmen who could make an impact early in their careers.

Here’s a more in-depth look at what Campbell said on Thursday.

Team identity

With the team still coming together to function effectively in the Penn State system, Campbell noted that he’s been learning more about the team every time they hit the field and will likely continue to discover new things in the first few weeks of the season.

“You got a new coaching staff, you got new players,” Campbell said. “So I think every day why we're continuing to pound away with the value of consistency and playing to a standard of excellence because that’s what 60 minutes in the game brings you.”

For the coaching staff, the offseason has been about training the players to handle external factors, such as playing at Beaver Stadium under the lights, in different weather conditions. Practice hasn’t been the final test of the team’s maximum capabilities.

Instead of trying to focus on the details that gameday brings, Campbell’s leaning more into which players are more mature and have stronger mental fortitude.

Should a player be lacking in that regard, Campbell has made it a point to help players build mental toughness for when the season kicks off.

“Every single day we're learning a little bit more about ourselves,” Campbell said. “Who can do it to the standard that we want to play the game of football with, and play to the standards that we set on this football program of what it takes to play championship level football here.”

All offseason long, Campbell has preached consistency above all else, and it’s a player’s ability to remain consistent day-in and day-out that he’s got his eyes on.

Offensive depth

Campbell spoke with great enthusiasm about the depth of two particular groups: the tight ends and the running backs.

He gave kudos to Andrew Rappleyea and Benjamin Brahmer for their efforts throughout the offseason, said that Finn Furmanek has had “his best couple of days” and Cooper Alexander is in a great spot as a depth piece. Campbell noted the quarterbacks are viewing the tight ends as “key pieces” in the offense thus far in fall camp.

“We're super excited about that group,” Campbell said. “Those guys have made awesome plays.”

Additionally, Gabe Burkle is working individually at practice, rehabbing a knee injury that ended his 2025 season. Campbell said that they’ll be eyeing his availability closer to the beginning of the season, but that the coaching staff is taking it slow with him.

As for the running backs, Campbell has been pleased with the four-man unit of Carson Hansen, James Peoples, Quinton Martin Jr. and Cam Wallace. He expects to get a lot of usage out of them throughout the season in some capacity, whether it be as running backs or on special teams.

“We hope we're playing for the long haul, and the reality is at that position you're going to need a lot of them,” Campbell said. "It's rare that you find tailbacks that can do all the things within the offense. They can all pass protect. They can all run. They can all catch.”

Freshman impact

With a largely veteran roster that’s transferred in or returned from last year’s team, Campbell was asked about this season’s crop of freshmen and how they can potentially make an impact early in their careers.

Campbell said that Jackson Ford, Josiah Zayas and Amarion Jackson are the freshmen separating themselves throughout the offseason.

“I talk about Zayas — I think he's made big plays every single practice that he's been here,” Campbell said. “Every single day that guy has showed up and he's got this unique trait that he can do a lot of things.”

Zayas had a pick six at Blue-White Practice this spring, and Campbell said that he had a great showing at Saturday’s scrimmage as well. Although Zayas is officially listed as a cornerback, Campbell said that he can place him in other spots depending on the team’s needs, including safety and at the nickel position.

“You're looking for guys that keep showing up and prove that they can play,” Campbell said about the select freshmen. “And they've got the mental fortitude to handle camp and to handle the defensive installation, the special teams installation, the offense installation, and those guys have certainly stuck out in a positive way for sure.”

title: ‘Anyone can be anywhere’ | Penn State LBs buying into versatility of group
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s linebacker room will have a different look in 2026, but the unit will showcase the same strengths that previous editions of linebacker rooms in Happy Valley have for so many years.

With the return of Tony Rojas, who’s as athletic as any player on the team, and the addition of three Iowa State linebackers, the linebackers have bought into the idea of being a versatile group, which only adds ammunition to D’Anton Lynn’s defensive scheme on a week-by-week basis.

“I think when you watch some really good defenses, whether it's college or the NFL, you have guys that can do so many different things,” linebacker Cael Brezina said at local media day on Aug. 7.

Penn State’s likely to throw a mix of players out there, including Rojas and Brezina, but Kooper Ebel, Caleb Bacon and Alex Tatsch will also see snaps. With Bacon testing out playing at defensive end during fall camp, it shows even more that the linebacker room is versatile.

While there could be upwards of five different linebackers playing in a single game, they specialize in all three of the positions, which could make the defense even more effective in the first year under Lynn.

Ebel said “a ton of the guys” in the room can play multiple positions. With that comes different ways for the defense to confuse opposing offenses, and it builds a recipe for success across the entire defense — every linebacker has bought into the system and knows their full athleticism is being utilized.

Penn State’s linebacker room has made for some superstars at the collegiate level. From all the way back to Jack Ham and LaVar Arrington, to more recently with Paul Posluszny and Michael Mauti. Add on Micah Parsons and Abdul Carter, the Nittany Lions have produced and developed elite linebackers who’ve all been versatile.

The versatility that was shown in prior stars is also what is being taught to the new players in the latest era of the program.

“You might be playing the same defense, you're playing the same cover three, but anyone can be anywhere, and I think that makes the defense really good and really multiple and really hard on the offense,” Brezina said. “So just having guys like that, and all of us being able to do different things is really powerful each of the times.”

No matter which combination of linebackers are on the field, there’s expectation that all of them can play at any position. The unit has grown in depth with redshirt freshman Cam Smith even showing out to some of the older players in the group, while also allowing all the starters to shift around on defense and make plays.

“To be able to have linebackers in our room who are willing and able to go do those things, obviously at the linebacker position and then on special teams, man, we want every guy in our room to travel. So we're trying to fill up all those spots,” Ebel said.

title: Position preview | New faces join Ryan Barker in Penn State’s 2026 special teams squad
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Similar to the rest of the roster, Penn State’s special teams room looks very different compared to how it did last year.

While the Nittany Lions returned their star placekicker and had their backup long snapper rise to the starting position, Penn State’s kickoff specialist and punter are transfers looking to make an impact in the Big Ten.

Additionally, the punt and kick returners aren’t set in stone, but there are plenty of options for special teams coordinator Justin Lustig to keep up with throughout fall camp.

Here’s how the special teams department is shaping up ahead of the 2026 season.

Placekicker

Ryan Barker took over the role as the starting placekicker just a few games into his redshirt freshman year and never looked back. After two-consecutive All-Big Ten honorable mention campaigns, the now redshirt junior earned himself a spot on the Lou Groza Award watch list.

Barker was one of most consistent kickers in the country last year, breaking the Nittany Lions’ single-season record in field goal percentage with a 94.7% completion rate, and his 89.2% career percentage currently ranks first all-time at Penn State. He also only missed a single extra point on 45 attempts.

“I'm a big believer in the ‘one shot, one kill’ mentality, which is Coach Lustig's motto.” Barker said at local media day on Aug. 7. “I've really adopted that since he's been around me for the past now through going on three years.”

Redshirt freshman Matthew Parker will likely be sitting behind Barker for the second straight season. The walk-on from York, Pennsylvania, got to play in last season's home opener against Nevada where he successfully converted on an extra point.

Kickoff specialist

With Gabe Nwosu graduating, the kickoff specialist position was left wide open going into the offseason. In comes Cristiano Rosa, a transfer from James Madison, to fill that role.

Rosa had been the Dukes’ primary kickoff specialist for the past two seasons after transferring from Central Connecticut State, where he’d only seen action in one game as a true freshman.

In 2025, Rosa struck 90 kickoffs with 62 of them being touchbacks, averaging 63 yards per kickoff. The year before, he took 69 kickoffs including 52 touchbacks with a near-identical average at 63.9 yards.

Punter

Sophomore Nathan Tiyce follows in the footsteps of former Nittany Lion Riley Thompson as the newest Australian-born punter at Penn State.

“Riley set a massive legacy here that I've got to try and fulfill,” Tiyce said at local media day. “Trying to meet those standards and the expectations that this program holds, and just ultimately just make the guys that have come before me proud.”

A transfer from Mississippi State, Tiyce saw action in nine games and made 12 punts. He finished his true freshman outing averaging 39 yards per punt with seven landing inside the 20-yard line and two sailing over 50 yards.

Battling Tiyce for the starting job is freshman Lucas Tenbrock, the No. 1 punter in the Class of 2026 per Chris Sailer Kicking, and the No. 5 punter per 247Sports composite. While Tiyce is currently projected to start, Lustig told 247Sports on August 12 that Tenbrock is “chasing him.”

Long snapper

Blaise Sokach-Minnick is next in line for the starting long snapper position in the wake of Tyler Duzansky, who signed with the Las Vegas Raiders as an undrafted free agent.

Sokach-Minnick has appeared in two games in each of the last three seasons at Penn State. Now a redshirt senior, he’s ready to inherit the starting role after spending four years on the bench behind Duzansky and 2022 Patrick Mannelly Award winner Chris Stoll, being named to the award’s watch list himself.

Redshirt sophomore Andrew Dufault will be the backup to start the season, having only appeared in two games so far.

Returners

The team’s kick and punt returner spots are currently in contest, however, there are a few names that are in the mix to make a push for the positions.

Cornerback Zion Tracy has the most experience on the team returning punts, although last year he didn’t make any attempts with the position held by wide receivers Trebor Pena and Devonte Ross. Tracy was the primary punt returner in 2024, averaging 5.8 yards per punt return on 15 attempts.

Zay Robinson, Koby Howard and Chase Sowell are in the mix to push Tracy for the position, as they’ve been seen taking reps there at practice. Robinson, Howard, Audavion Collins, James Peoples, Carson Hansen and Quinton Martin Jr., meanwhile, have been the kick returners during fall camp.

title: Penn State men's soccer kicks off Rob Dow era with matchups against Mercyhurst, Missouri State
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Rob Dow era is finally here for Penn State.

The Nittany Lions will face their first tests of the season this week as they face Mercyhurst at 7 p.m. on Thursday before traveling to face Missouri State at 8 p.m. on Sunday.

Here’s a look at what to expect from Penn State in its first season with a new coaching staff.

Mercyhurst

This year marks the second all-time matchup between the Nittany Lions and Mercyhurst following Penn State’s 5-0 beatdown last season.

Defender Morgan Marshall was the only goalscorer from the starting 11, but Penn State added another four goals in the final 35 minutes via its bench.

For Penn State, it will be opening an era under Dow, a coach who led Vermont to a national championship in 2024. While a national title in Year 1 is a big ask, a loss in his first game coaching the Nittany Lions would be a poor start to a heavily anticipated season.

Penn State’s roster has a completely different look than last year, returning just three athletes from the year before.

Defenders Joe Sheridan and Marshall come back to Happy Valley for their second and fourth seasons, respectively. Both were starters for the Nittany Lions in 2025, tallying a combined 29 starts.

However, the Nittany Lions also added many new faces that will take the field this season. In addition to several freshman additions, Dow’s squad added numerous international students and NCAA transfers.

Among the new names are British Columbia’s Joven Mann, Duquesne’s Grant McIntosh and Loughborough’s Sam Fielding. Mann brings three years of midfield experience as a senior, while McIntosh and Fielding are both graduate transfers.

Mercyhurst is coming off a struggling 3-10-4 after tallying just 18 goals during the season. However, its top goalscorers, Santiago Giraldo and Benjamin Buckley, are back for another year and will look to carry their squad again.

Missouri State

Penn State and Missouri State have only faced each other twice in school history, resulting in a split 1-1 record. The Nittany Lions emerged with a 1-0 victory in 2001, while the Bears won 3-1 in University Park last season.

Missouri State put together a 6-6-4 record last season, good enough for a spot in the American Conference Championship. However, it will be without top goalscorer Fumiya Shiraishi, who led the team with eight goals last season — twice as many as the next-best player.

Now, the Bears will be led by Spanish fifth-year forward Diego Real. Despite starting just four games last season, the Valencia native finished second on the team with four goals.

Another missing piece for Missouri State will come at goalkeeper. After relying on Will Lowry with his 25 saves in 10 starts last season, both he and backup goalie Jonathan Kliewer have both graduated.

Goalkeeper duties will now be placed onto Iona transfer Fernando Alves Schmelz and sophomore Danny Cullum.

The Nittany Lions also have a trio of inexperienced goalies, likely leading to Fredrick Grundin — it’s third and final returner from 2025 — to take over in net. The Swedish native played 270 minutes last season and allowed six goals against zero saves.

Fortunately for Penn State, its matchup with the Bears is its second contest of the season, allowing Grundin or the other two keepers a chance to enter Sunday’s game with some experience.

title: Penn State women’s soccer looks for 1st win against West Virginia
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
After opening the season with a tie against the No. 2 team in the country last week, Penn State is back for another chance to enter the win column.

The Nittany Lions will face West Virginia at 7 p.m. on Thursday, marking the last road trip before the season opener on Aug. 27.

Penn State offers a much different starting lineup this season, but has shown this year’s squad is capable of big moments. Here’s a look at what to expect from Thursday’s matchup.

Matchup history

The Mountaineers have been a staple of Penn State’s nonconference schedule, having faced each other every year since 2009, excluding the canceled season due to COVID-19. During that timeframe, in addition to a few matchups played in earlier years, the Nittany Lions hold a dominant, 15-7-3 record.

West Virginia hasn’t emerged victorious since 2017, when it won 2-1 in Morgantown. Besides a 1-1 tie in 2019, the blue and white has won every game over the past 10 years.

In 2021 and 2022, Penn State held the Mountaineers to three straight shutouts, winning 2-0 during the 2021 and 2022 regular seasons and 4-0 in the 2022 NCAA Tournament.

The Nittany Lions won last year’s matchup, 3-1, with goals from Hannah Jordan, Amelia White and Julia Raich.

2026 Mountaineers

West Virginia opened its season last Thursday with a 2-0 victory against Dayton. In front of the home crowd, the Mountaineers dominated the second half to start 2026 undefeated.

Just 54 seconds after halftime, Sophia Nickel positioned herself with a scoring opportunity and was fed the ball by Maya Leoni, putting the first point of the season on the board for West Virginia.

Seventeen minutes later, the Mountaineers capitalized again, this time scoring off of a corner kick.

While West Virginia goalkeeper Bailey Herfurth recorded a clean slate in her final season opener, she didn’t face much pressure. Dayton had just one shot on target, with five total shots the entire game.

Thursday’s contest

Penn State entered the 2026 season unranked, receiving just nine votes in the United Soccer Coaches poll. However, it tied No. 2 Notre Dame last week, and will look to earn its place in the poll after its second game of the season this week.

The Nittany Lions operated through junior midfielder Aubrey Kulpa last Thursday, who appears to be one of the team’s go-to players this season.

After playing just 15 games last year due to a long-term injury, Kulpa kicked off her junior season with a goal and an assist, helping Penn State to a 2-0 lead less than 10 minutes after halftime.

Goalkeeper Mackenzie Gress needed just one save to keep the Fighting Irish off the board in the first half, but let two goals in during the second half. Her three second-half saves kept the score even after the final whistle.

Without Amelia White, Olivia Borgen, Kaitlyn MacBean or Raich this season, the Nittany Lions have had to turn to some of its younger stars. In addition to Kulpa’s success, Paige Kalal scored the team’s other goal with her five total shots.

title: Big Ten offseason roundup | Freshmen, quarterbacks headline summer in conference
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The college football season begins in just under two weeks, with Week 0 kicking things off.

The Big Ten has had the last three national champions, with plenty of talented teams this year that could make it four years in a row for the conference. Additionally, the depth of the conference continues to grow stronger.

From freshmen standouts to notable veteran quarterbacks, the Big Ten has been a big part of the talk of the country leading up to the 2026 season.

Freshmen phenoms

The Big Ten ushered in some of the top players from the 2026 class, and those guys have already started to make a name for themselves on their respective teams.

For USC — who brought in the top recruiting class in the nation — a player from each side of the ball has opened eyes. Wide receiver Boobie Feaster has been making highlight reel catches in practices, while defensive end Luke Wafle could see the field early on in his collegiate career.

Oregon brought in two highly regarded freshmen on the offensive line. Immanuel Iheanacho and Tommy Tofi could both see impactful minutes in their first years, as both Iheanacho and Tofi entered Eugene with a college build and have impressed early in fall camp.

On the eastern side of the conference, Michigan and Ohio State both have a freshman who’s fighting to see early playing time. The Wolverines are likely to trot out freshman running back Savion Hiter, who was the top incoming running back, according to 247Sports composite.

Ohio State has a 5-star of its own who’s expected to see the field in cornerback Jay Timmons, who has lost his black stripe on his helmet and has been seeing starting reps at the nickel spot.

As the season begins, other freshmen could make headlines and be featured in offenses, as teams continue to develop their young stars.

Veteran quarterbacks

The Big Ten will be headlined by veteran quarterbacks across the conference, as every expected top team will feature a quarterback who’s played at least one season as a starter.

Oregon’s Dante Moore, Ohio State’s Julian Sayin, USC’s Jayden Maiava, UCLA’s Nico Iamaleava, Michigan’s Bryce Underwood and Washington’s Demond Williams Jr. all are returning to their teams as starters from a season ago.

However, newcomer veterans have found their stride early in the year. Indiana’s Josh Hoover, Penn State’s Rocco Becht, Nebraska’s Anthony Colandrea and Illinois’ Katin Houser have all become accustomed to their new teams.

With a heavy emphasis on older quarterbacks starting to take over in college football, the Big Ten will feature some of the best, as Hoover, Maiava, Moore and Sayin all are amongst the favorites to win the Heisman Trophy.

“The Game” controversy

Arguably the biggest rivalry in the entire sport, The Game, featuring Ohio State and Michigan, is played annually to close out the regular season.

Michigan’s new coach, Kyle Whittingham commented on the rivalry, wondering if the team has a better chance if it hates the opponent or not. While that may take away from what has been known as a heated rivalry, Whittingham later admitted that he wanted to beat the Buckeyes more than any other team in the country, given that the rivalry and game is “of the utmost importance.”

Ohio State made an adjustment to its schedule to have full focus on the rivalry game. The Buckeyes moved their Senior Day festivities to the first week of the season, so that the final game day can be focused on defeating the Wolverines.

While the NIL and transfer portal era could change up how rivalries are viewed, even with a new coach at the helm of the Wolverines, “The Game” is still seen as the biggest rivalry in college sports.

Impactful injuries

Two injuries could have a significant impact on teams’ success. Maryland defensive end Zahir Mathis is expected to miss the entire 2026 season with an injury. The Terrapins are expected to turn to 5-star edge rusher Zion Elee to fill in for Mathis, but the absence of one of their top pass rushers from last year will still hinder the defense’s success.

USC will be without its starting center Kilian O’Connor for the 2026 campaign. O’Connor made seven starts at center last year and was expected to be the full-time starter in the middle of the Trojans’ offensive line.

title: Department of Defense reportedly orders Penn State to review ties to ‘foreign entities’ or lose funding

The U.S. Department of Defense issued a public release ordering 30 academic institutions to review their ties and collaborations with "foreign entities of concern" on Monday.

The institutions will have until Aug. 31 to complete the audit in order to remain eligible for federal research funding. The release did not include the names of the institutions. However, The Guardian and Fox News both reported they received a list of the institutions notified from an unnamed U.S. official, and it includes Penn State.

“Penn State received notice from the Department of War to conduct a research security audit and has communicated to the department that that work is under way,” Wyatt Dubois, a Penn State spokesperson, said via email. “The University greatly values its relationship with the Department of War and shares its commitment to maintaining the highest standards in national security, research security and scientific integrity."

The audit requires the institutions to identify foreign collaborations, assess exposure of sensitive research and end partnerships the government deems problematic.

"The Department of War has zero tolerance for academic partnerships that compromise our national security," Emil Michael, under secretary of war for research and engineering, said in the release. "Institutions that receive funding from American taxpayers must uphold the highest standards of research security, and these mandated audits will ensure accountability across the board."

Last month, Penn State and the U.S. Army signed a 10-year partnernship agreement in which the university will provide research and engineering support services to the Army.

title: ‘Building it off what we’re best at’ | D’Anton Lynn’s defensive scheme puts Penn State players in control
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
When Tony Rojas announced his return to Penn State under Matt Campbell, he knew he’d be under the leadership of his fourth defensive coordinator in as many years.

Rojas started his career under Manny Diaz before working with Tom Allen and Jim Knowles over the next two years. As he takes the field for his redshirt junior season, he’ll now be led by D’Anton Lynn, who has had to build his defensive scheme from scratch.

“He’s just building it off us and what we’re best at,” Rojas said at local media day on Aug. 7. “It’s just calling the plays on how we want it.”

Penn State’s defense features many playmakers. In addition to Rojas, Zion Tracy, Kooper Ebel and Jeremiah Cooper have emerged as key pieces for Lynn.

Under Lynn’s new system, those players won’t simply be expected to fit into a predetermined scheme. Instead, Lynn has emphasized understanding the defense’s core concepts and allowing his players to take ownership of it.

“Really starting from the ground up,” Lynn said at local media day. “With the staff, as we go through the defense, we try to rebuild it from scratch as far as each coverage, each concept. We’re gonna talk about how everyone did it, and now what’s the best way that we can do it here.”

That process began in the spring, when Lynn and his staff deliberately slowed down the installation. As training camp progressed, the pace increased.

“Our biggest thing is we want guys to really understand the core concepts because we feel like if they can get an understanding of it, that’s easier for them to buy in,” Lynn said.

For Lynn, that understanding is what eventually allows players to take control, saying “at some point in time, they need to take the keys.”

That player-led philosophy has resonated with the players, as has the simplistic installation of the defense during the spring.

“I like his style,” Tracy said. “It’s simple, but it’s complex at the same time. It’s a good vibe.”

Because of the defense’s simplicity, the transition to a fourth defensive coordinator may actually be less difficult than it appears for Tracy and Rojas.

Lynn said Rojas and Tracy have picked up his defense faster than he’s anticipated, allowing them to help mentor other players and aid them in learning the scheme.

However, it’s not just the players who have spent the offseason learning Lynn’s defense. The new position coaches have been in the same boat, and Lynn has relied on others to help him in the process, including veteran coach Terry Smith.

“Terry’s been here a while and has been a part of really good defenses here,” Lynn said. “Just getting his input, whether it’s something about the defense or whether it’s just something about our players, he’s a very insightful coach.”

Now, with three weeks until the season begins, the question will be whether Lynn’s player-led approach can translate from the practice field to Saturdays and bring Penn State’s new-look defense together when it matters most.
